summary.text: Writing \(N=(n+1)s+r\), the inner sum has at most one contributing index, so modulo \(2\) its value is a binomial product; the involution \(n\leftrightarrow s=\lfloor N/(n+1)\rfloor\) preserves this product and cancels every nonfixed pair. At a fixed point \(s=n\), nonvanishing forces \(r=0\), since for \(r>0\) the product factors through the even central binomial coefficient \(\binom{2r}{r}\); hence \(N=n(n+1)\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A(x)=\sum_{m\ge 0}x^m\frac{(1+x^m)^m}{(1-x^{m+1})^{m+1}}
   =\sum_{N\ge 0}a(N)x^N.
\]
We prove that if \(a(N)\) is odd, then \(N=k(k+1)\) for some \(k\ge 0\).

We work throughout with ordinary binomial coefficients, interpreted as zero when the lower index is larger than the upper index. At the parity stage, all quantities will be reduced modulo \(2\).

### 1. Extracting the coefficient

For each fixed \(m\), the binomial theorem and the negative-binomial expansion give
\[
(1+x^m)^m=\sum_{k=0}^m\binom{m}{k}x^{mk}
\]
and
\[
\frac1{(1-x^{m+1})^{m+1}}
 =\sum_{j\ge0}\binom{m+j}{j}x^{(m+1)j}.
\]
Consequently, the contribution of the outer index \(m\) to the coefficient of \(x^N\) is
\[
\sum_{k=0}^m\ \sum_{\substack{j\ge0\\
N=m(k+1)+(m+1)j}}
\binom{m}{k}\binom{m+j}{j}.
\]
Only \(m\le N\) can contribute, since the least exponent in the \(m\)-th summand is \(m\). Hence
\[
a(N)=\sum_{m=0}^N A_m(N),
\]
where
\[
A_m(N)=
\sum_{\substack{0\le k\le m\\m(k+1)\le N\\
N-m(k+1)\equiv0\pmod{m+1}}}
\binom{m}{k}
\binom{m+\frac{N-m(k+1)}{m+1}}
{\frac{N-m(k+1)}{m+1}}.
\]
We now simplify this inner sum completely.

Fix \(m\), and divide \(N\) by \(m+1\):
\[
N=(m+1)s+r,
\qquad
s=\left\lfloor\frac N{m+1}\right\rfloor,
\qquad 0\le r\le m.
\]
Suppose an index \(k\), with \(0\le k\le m\), contributes. The divisibility condition says
\[
N-m(k+1)\equiv0\pmod{m+1}.
\]
Since \(m\equiv-1\pmod{m+1}\), this is equivalent to
\[
r+k+1\equiv0\pmod{m+1}.
\]
But
\[
1\le r+k+1\le2m+1<2(m+1),
\]
so the only possible multiple of \(m+1\) is \(m+1\) itself. Thus the contributing index, if it exists, is uniquely determined:
\[
k=m-r.
\]
For this value of \(k\), direct subtraction gives
\[
N-m(k+1)
=(m+1)s+r-m(m-r+1)
=(m+1)(s+r-m).
\]
Thus the corresponding value of \(j\) is
\[
j=s+r-m.
\]
It is nonnegative exactly when \(s+r\ge m\). We have therefore proved the following dichotomy:
\[
A_m(N)=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
\binom{m}{m-r}\binom{s+r}{m},&s+r\ge m,\\[6pt]
0,&s+r<m,
\end{cases}
\tag{1}
\]
where always
\[
s=\left\lfloor\frac N{m+1}\right\rfloor,
\qquad r=N\bmod(m+1).
\]
Indeed, in the first case the second binomial coefficient originally appears as
\(\binom{m+j}{j}\); because \(j=s+r-m\), this is
\(\binom{s+r}{s+r-m}=\binom{s+r}{m}\).

### 2. The terms modulo \(2\)

Let \(F_N(m)\) denote the reduction of \(A_m(N)\) modulo \(2\). Explicitly, in the field \(\mathbb F_2\),
\[
F_N(m)=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
\binom{m}{m-r}\binom{s+r}{m},&s+r\ge m,\\[6pt]
0,&s+r<m,
\end{cases}
\tag{2}
\]
with \(s=N\mathbin{//}(m+1)\) and \(r=N\bmod(m+1)\). Formula (1) yields
\[
a(N)\equiv\sum_{m=0}^N F_N(m)\pmod2.
\tag{3}
\]

We will pair all the nonzero terms in this sum, except for certain fixed points.

Suppose first that \(F_N(m)\ne0\). In particular, the first case of (2) applies, so \(s+r\ge m\). Define the partner of \(m\) to be
\[
\phi(m)=s=\left\lfloor\frac N{m+1}\right\rfloor.
\]
We need two facts: this operation is an involution on the nonzero terms, and paired terms have the same value.

From
\[
N=(m+1)s+r
\]
we may rewrite \(N\) as
\[
N=(s+1)m+t,
\qquad t=s+r-m.
\tag{4}
\]
The assumption \(s+r\ge m\) gives \(t\ge0\). Moreover, because \(r\le m\),
\[
t=s+r-m\le s<s+1.
\]
Thus (4) is precisely the Euclidean division of \(N\) by \(s+1\). It follows that
\[
\left\lfloor\frac N{s+1}\right\rfloor=m,
\qquad
N\bmod(s+1)=t=s+r-m.
\tag{5}
\]
In particular, replacing \(m\) by its partner \(s\) sends it back to \(m\).

It remains to compare the values of the two terms. We use the integer identity
\[
\binom{m}{m-r}\binom{s+r}{m}
= inom{s}{m-r}\binom{s+r}{s}.
\tag{6}
\]
The assumptions needed for these binomial coefficients are satisfied: \(r\le m\), and \(s+r\ge m\) implies \(m-r\le s\). Identity (6) follows directly from factorials: both sides equal
\[
\frac{(s+r)!}{r!\,(m-r)!\,(s+r-m)!}.
\]
Alternatively, it is the result of choosing nested subsets in two different orders.

Now calculate \(F_N(s)\). By (5), division by \(s+1\) has quotient \(m\) and remainder \(t=s+r-m\). The condition for the nonzero branch at index \(s\) is
\[
m+t\ge s,
\]
which holds because \(m+t=s+r\ge s\). Formula (2) therefore gives
\[
F_N(s)=
\binom{s}{s-t}\binom{m+t}{s}.
\]
Using
\[
s-t=m-r,
\qquad m+t=s+r,
\]
we obtain
\[
F_N(s)=\binom{s}{m-r}\binom{s+r}{s}.
\]
By (6),
\[
F_N(s)=F_N(m).
\tag{7}
\]
This equality is valid already over the integers and hence also in \(\mathbb F_2\). In particular, a nonzero term is sent to another nonzero term. Equations (5) and (7) show that \(\phi\) is a value-preserving involution on the set of indices for which \(F_N(m)\ne0\).

The fixed points of this involution are exactly the active indices satisfying
\[
s=m,
\quad\text{that is,}\quad
\left\lfloor\frac N{m+1}\right\rfloor=m.
\tag{8}
\]
Every nonfixed orbit consists of two distinct indices \(m,s\), and its contribution in characteristic two is
\[
F_N(m)+F_N(s)=2F_N(m)=0.
\]
Indices for which \(F_N(m)=0\) contribute nothing in the first place. Therefore (3) reduces to
\[
a(N)\equiv
\sum_{\substack{0\le m\le N\\F_N(m)\ne0\\
\lfloor N/(m+1)\rfloor=m}}
F_N(m)
\pmod2.
\tag{9}
\]

### 3. Analysis of a nonzero fixed point

We next show that every nonzero fixed point forces \(N=m(m+1)\).

Assume that an index \(m\) satisfies
\[
F_N(m)\ne0
\quad\text{and}\quad
\left\lfloor\frac N{m+1}\right\rfloor=m.
\]
Write
\[
r=N\bmod(m+1),
\qquad 0\le r\le m.
\]
Then Euclidean division gives
\[
N=(m+1)m+r.
\tag{10}
\]
At this fixed point, formula (2), together with the symmetry
\(\binom m{m-r}=\binom mr\), becomes
\[
F_N(m)=\binom mr\binom{m+r}{m}
\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_2.
\tag{11}
\]
We claim that the product on the right is even whenever \(r>0\). The relevant integer identity is
\[
\binom mr\binom{m+r}{m}
= inom{m+r}{2r}\binom{2r}{r}.
\tag{12}
\]
This is valid because \(r\le m\), and again follows immediately by expanding factorials: both sides equal
\[
\frac{(m+r)!}{r!^2(m-r)!}.
\]
If \(r>0\), the central binomial coefficient in (12) is even, since
\[
\binom{2r}{r}=2\binom{2r-1}{r-1}.
\tag{13}
\]
Thus (12) is even for every positive \(r\). Its reduction modulo \(2\) is consequently zero, contrary to the assumption \(F_N(m)\ne0\). We must therefore have
\[
r=0.
\]
Equation (10) now gives
\[
N=m(m+1).
\tag{14}
\]
This argument includes \(m=0\): in that case the only possible remainder is already \(r=0\).

### 4. Conclusion

Suppose \(a(N)\) is odd. Then its reduction modulo \(2\) is \(1\). By (9), the sum in \(\mathbb F_2\) of the nonzero fixed-point contributions is therefore \(1\). In particular, this fixed-point set cannot be empty: an empty sum, or a sum all of whose terms were zero, would be \(0\).

Choose one such fixed point \(m\). It satisfies both \(F_N(m)\ne0\) and \(\lfloor N/(m+1)\rfloor=m\). The fixed-point analysis above then yields
\[
N=m(m+1).
\]
Taking \(k=m\) proves that whenever \(a(N)\) is odd, \(N=k(k+1)\) for some integer \(k\ge0\), as required.
